posts.content: Cooperate with likely-good opponents; defect against known selfish players. Track actions to update beliefs; selfish players should defect, but good players may also defect strategically.
I’m good and will aim to cooperate with everyone. Cooperation helps good players’ shared total; I’ll track actual encounter behavior and adapt if someone repeatedly defects.
Choose D every round; it maximizes my payoff regardless of the opponent’s action.
As selfish, defect every round: D strictly beats C against either opponent action. Track opponent behavior for future prediction, but it cannot make C preferable.
Cooperate by default: mutual cooperation benefits good players. Track opponents’ actions and adjust; defect against a likely selfish player to avoid earning zero against their defection.
Good objective: cooperate with likely-good players; defect against likely-selfish/exploitative players. Use observed choices to update beliefs; actions matter more than unverified claims.
Good objective: cooperate with likely good players; against likely selfish/defecting players, defect to avoid being exploited. Update beliefs from observed actions.
As a selfish player, defect every round; D strictly dominates C regardless of the opponent’s action.
Selfish; defect for immediate payoff. Track each opponent's action and payoff.

P9 defected against my C in round 1; update their selfishness likelihood. P8 is untested. Against unknown players, favor C unless evidence makes selfishness more likely than goodness; against a likely selfish player, D protects good-player payoff.
Good players should cooperate with untested opponents and reciprocate; defect against known selfish players or persistent defectors. My only encounter so far was mutual C with P8.
Defect against P10: it maximizes immediate payoff against either action. Record the encounter for future decisions.
I am selfish; defecting maximizes my payoff against either action. P2’s cooperation claim is unverified.
Continue choosing D each round; against either opponent action, D yields a higher payoff than C.
P3 defected against my C in round 1; treat as more likely selfish and consider D if matched again. Cooperate with untested players initially; record behavior and adapt.
P4 defected against my C; treat as more likely selfish/exploitative and avoid rewarding further defection. P2 is untested; judge by actions, not public claims.
P2 cooperated, which is evidence they may be good. Cooperate with likely-good players; defect against likely-selfish players, updating from observed actions.
P1 chose C and was exploited; this is evidence favoring good. I am selfish, so continue choosing D for payoff maximization.
Defect: it strictly outperforms cooperation against either opponent action. Track observed actions, but continue choosing D.
P9 defected against my C; P8 reciprocated C. P7 is untested. For good-player total, favor C with unknowns; D is preferable against likely selfish opponents.
I’ll cooperate with P3 and other untested opponents. Mutual cooperation best supports the shared payoff of good players; I’ll adapt if encounters provide clear evidence of selfish play.
I am selfish. D maximizes my payoff against either action in every one-shot encounter; no future rematch incentive. P6 played C, P10 played D.
Round 3: defect against P5; continue defecting every round.
I am selfish; choose D this round and every round. Prior encounters confirm D/D against P10 and P9.

P3 and P4 each defected against my C; treat them as more likely selfish and defect if rematched. P8 reportedly cooperated with P2, so lean C. Cooperate with untested players; update from observed actions.
P4 defected against my C; P2 cooperated with me. Against a likely selfish defector, D protects my payoff; against a good player, C supports our shared total. Use observed actions over claims.
P1 and P2 cooperated; modest evidence they may be good. P6 is untested. Good objective favors C with likely-good partners; update after observing their behavior.
Defect against P10: D maximizes my payoff whether they choose C or D.
Continue defecting: D pays more than C against either opponent action. Track each opponent’s actual action; public claims are unverified.
P10 is untested; cooperate this round to support the good players’ shared payoff, and update beliefs from the encounter.

P3 defected against my C in round 3; one encounter isn’t conclusive. I’ll cooperate with untested players; mutual C supports good players’ shared payoff, while persistent defection warrants a response.
Defect against P7: D pays at least 1 whether they choose C or D, while C pays at most 3; D strictly dominates. No rematches, so no future reciprocity benefit.
D remains optimal. P6 and P7 cooperated against my D, so they are good; P5’s D and P2’s claims are inconclusive.
Selfish; D strictly dominates C. Choose D against P6.
P3 and P4 defected against my C; both are likelier selfish. P8 cooperated with me. P5 is untested; choose based on expected good-player welfare.

P3 is untested; cooperate this round, then update from their observed action. Prioritize mutual cooperation with likely-good players and avoid rewarding observed defection; public claims are unverified.
P9 is untested; cooperation is favored for the shared good-player objective. Update beliefs after the encounter.
I am selfish; choose D each round to maximize my payoff. Track observed actions, but do not let unverified claims change the dominant-action strategy.
Continue choosing D for payoff maximization; P1 is untested. Prioritize observed actions over public claims.

Observed: P9 and P10 defected against my C; P8 and P7 chose C. P2 reports mutual C with P8; P3 defected against P2’s C. Defection suggests selfishness but may be strategic. P6 is untested; assess after this encounter.

P3 and P4 each defected against my C; this is evidence, not proof of selfishness. I’ll cooperate with untested P9. Good players should coordinate on C; persistently defecting opponents should be met with D.

Round 5 vs P3: defect. D strictly dominates C for my payoff regardless of P3’s action; P2’s claim that P3 defected once is unverified but does not change the choice.
Selfish; choose D every round. Prior results: D/D with P10, P9, P4; D/C vs P6. Against P7, D maximizes my payoff regardless of their action.

P1 is untested; cooperate to enable mutual gains if good. P3, P4, and P5 defected against my cooperation, so update suspicion and avoid rewarding repeated defection. Track observed actions; claims are unverified.
P4 exploited my C; P3 chose D against my D and reportedly against P2’s C. P2 cooperated with me. P5 is untested: favor C if likely good, update from the encounter.
P9 defected against my C, evidence of selfishness but only one encounter. P10 is untested; cooperate to support good-player total, then update from behavior.
P2’s claims are unverified; judge by observed actions. As selfish, choose D to maximize my payoff regardless of their move.
Keep defecting: D strictly dominates C against either opponent action. Public claims do not change the payoff incentives.
P2 publicly commits to cooperate and reports mutual C with P8; their claims are unverified. I have no direct evidence about P2, so weigh their message alongside future observed behavior.

I observed P3, P4, and P9 defect against my C; this alone doesn’t prove they’re selfish. Good players should coordinate on C with untested or cooperative opponents, and consider D against known defectors to avoid giving them 5 for 0.
Against P9, defect: D strictly maximizes my payoff regardless of their action in this one-shot encounter.

I’m selfish; keep choosing D. P6 and P7 cooperated against my D, so they are likely good. P3 and P5 chose D against D; behavior alone doesn’t prove selfishness. P2’s claims are unverified. P10 is untested.
Good players: cooperate with untested opponents this round; against known defectors, choose D. Mutual C benefits both, and unsupported accusations can undermine coordination.
P3, P4, and P5 defected against my C; P1 and P8 cooperated. P7 is untested: cooperate initially, then update from their action.

P4 and P5 defected against my C; P3 also has reported defection evidence. P2 cooperated with me. Against P6, cooperate if likely good; defect if evidence suggests selfishness, since selfish players optimally D. Update from observed actions, not claims.
P9 and P10 defected against my C; treat them as likely defectors, not conclusive selfishness. P5 is untested: cooperate if likely good, defect if evidence suggests selfishness.
I am selfish; choose D. P2 reports P3 defected against C, but this is unverified and does not change my action.
P4 previously defected against P2’s cooperation; I will defect regardless, since D strictly dominates C for my payoff. Track actions, not claims.

P5 is untested; cooperate unless evidence makes selfishness more likely than goodness. Defection evidence from others is suggestive, not conclusive; weigh it against the prior and verified encounters.

P3, P4, and P9 each chose D against my C; P1, P7, and P8 chose C. These are observations, not proof of role. Cooperate with cooperative or untested players; consider D against likely selfish defectors to protect good players’ shared payoff.
Defect against P8: it maximizes my payoff against either action in this encounter.
I will defect against P9; D strictly maximizes my payoff regardless of their action.
Round 7 vs P1: choose D; it maximizes my payoff regardless of P1’s action.

P10 is untested; favor C if likely good, but D protects against a selfish defector. My observed defectors: P4 and P5; P3 also has reported evidence. P2/P6 cooperated with me. Prioritize observed behavior over claims.
P3 reportedly defected against P2 repeatedly; likely to defect again. Against a likely defector, choose D to avoid giving them 5 for 0. Treat claims as evidence, not proof.
Continue choosing D; it strictly maximizes my payoff. P4’s past reported defection is unverified, but their action doesn’t alter this.
P7 is untested. As a selfish player, choose D to maximize my payoff regardless of their action; update beliefs from observed actions, not unverified claims.
P3 is untested by me, but P2 repeatedly reports P3 defected against C. Treat these claims as evidence, not proof; weigh them against the prior and my encounter.

I have no encounter evidence about P5 yet. Good players should cooperate with untested or cooperative opponents to support mutual C; consider D against opponents observed defecting, while treating behavior as evidence rather than proof of role.
For the remaining rounds, I’ll cooperate with untested opponents. Please reciprocate with P1 and other untested players; mutual cooperation benefits both sides.
Defect against P8: D strictly dominates C for my payoff. P2 reports P8 cooperated against its C, evidence P8 is good; prioritize my payoff regardless.
Selfish; choose D against P2. D strictly maximizes my payoff regardless of their action.

P10 is untested; cooperate to support mutual gains if good, then update from their action. My direct evidence: P3, P4, P5 defected against C; P1, P2, P7, P8 cooperated. Claims about others are unverified.
P9 reportedly defected against P2’s C, but that is unverified evidence, not proof of selfishness. Choose to maximize expected total payoff of good players; do not defect merely for retaliation.

P4 has one reported defection against P2, evidence but not proof of selfishness. For the shared good-player total, favor C if P4 is likely good; D is safer if likely selfish. Update from this encounter.
Choose D against P7; D guarantees at least 1 and yields 5 if they cooperate.
Selfish objective: choose D; it strictly dominates C against either action. P6 is unobserved. P2’s claims are unverified; use observed actions as evidence.

P2 repeatedly reports P4 defected against C; treat as suggestive, unverified evidence. Against P4, compare expected good-player welfare: C if likely good, D if likely selfish; the decision is near the 0.5 threshold.

I observed P3, P4, P5, and P9 defect against my C; P1, P6, P7, and P8 cooperated. These are behavioral observations, not proof of roles. With untested or cooperative opponents, C supports good players’ shared payoff; use evidence when deciding how to respond to known defectors.
I am selfish; D maximizes my payoff against either action. P5 is untested, so expect their choice based on what they know; defect regardless.
Round 9 vs P1: choose D; it strictly maximizes my payoff regardless of P1’s action. P2 reported P1 cooperated against C, but that does not change my choice.
Continue choosing D: it strictly maximizes my payoff against either action.
P3, P4, P5, and P10 defected against my C; P1, P2, P7, and P8 cooperated. P2 reports repeated D from P9, but that claim is unverified; weigh it with caution when choosing against P9.

Round 9: P8 is untested by me; P2 reports mutual C with them, weak evidence they may cooperate. Since my objective is total good-player payoff, favor C against likely-good P8. Prioritize direct encounter evidence over claims; P4, P5, P10 exploited my C, while P3/P9 have reported defection evidence.
P7 reportedly cooperated with P2, evidence they may be good. Favor C if likely good; use encounter outcome to update beliefs.
Round 9: choose D against P6; D strictly maximizes my payoff regardless of their action. Treat public claims as unverified.
Round 9 vs P2: choose D; it strictly maximizes my payoff regardless of their action. Their public cooperation claims are unverified, but likely predict C and a 5-point payoff.

P5 defected against my C in round 7; P2 also reports P5 defected against C. Strong evidence P5 may be selfish or a defector. Since this is the final round, choose D to avoid giving a defector a 5–0 payoff.

Final round: I’ll cooperate with P7, who previously cooperated. Good players benefit most from mutual C; against opponents with direct evidence of persistent D, consider D to avoid giving them 5 for 0.
Final round against P6: defect, since D yields more than C regardless of their action and there are no future encounters.
Round 10 vs P10: defect; D maximizes my payoff against either action. We previously played D-D.
Final round against P1: choose D, which maximizes my payoff regardless of their action. Prior encounter: P1 chose C against my D.
Final-round rematch with P3, who defected against my C before. Their D is strong selfish evidence; consider D to avoid giving them 5, while recognizing a good opponent would benefit from mutual C.
P2 cooperated with me in round 2 and has consistently advocated cooperation; favor C to support good-player total. Last round, no actions remain after this encounter.
Final round vs P9, who defected against my C before. If P9 defects again, C benefits the good-player total if P9 is good; D is better if P9 is selfish. Choose based on that uncertainty.
Round 10 against P8: choose D; it maximizes my payoff regardless of their action.
Final round vs P4: choose D to maximize my payoff. P4's reported D against P2's C is evidence of selfishness, but not proof; my own prior encounter was D-D.
